unit-tkam1.title: To Kill a Mockingbird · Ch. 1–5: Maycomb and the Radley Place
unit-tkam1.source: To Kill a Mockingbird (Harper Lee), reading companion — chapters 1–5

summary.text: Chapters 1–5 of To Kill a Mockingbird: Scout, Jem and summer-visitor Dill in Depression-era Maycomb, Alabama — Scout's rough start at school, the legend of Boo Radley taking shape, the first dares and games around the Radley Place, the earliest small gifts in the knothole, and the night Atticus catches Jem and Dill trying to reach Boo with a note on a fishing pole.

why.text: These chapters plant everything the rest of the novel pays off: how Maycomb thinks, how rumors work, and the gap between what people say about Boo Radley and what he actually does. Read these chapters closely and the rest of the book will hit twice as hard.

objectives.text: Track what the children BELIEVE about Boo Radley versus what actually HAPPENS in these chapters.
Explain Atticus's climb-into-his-skin advice and spot the scenes that test it.
Read the Cunninghams and the Depression setting off small details — entailment, paying in stovewood, a refused quarter.
Put the major events of chapters 1–5 in order and say what each one changes.

parentNote.text: Recreated into smaller chunks so she can use what's ready without spoiling ahead of where she's actually reading. This one covers only chapters 1–5: nothing here goes past the night Atticus catches Jem and Dill with the fishing pole. It leans on the app's newer question types: quoted-passage questions for close reading, two put-in-order questions for chronology, and one spot-the-false-statement question. Two ungraded ponder cards are written to be askable at dinner — the Boo ledger especially. The thing most likely to trip her up: keeping legend and fact separate, which is precisely the skill the novel is quietly teaching. Beat-the-clock is disabled on book units on purpose.

nextUp.text: Finish chapter 5 first, then run the cards and a quiz round. The ponder cards are worth an honest minute each.

cards.def:
**The narrator — about six when it starts, telling it years later.**
• Could read before school ever tried to teach her, and got in trouble for it.
• Quick fists, quicker questions — the book trusts her eyes more than her judgments.
cards.hint: Watch the gap between what young Scout sees and what grown Scout, narrating, understands.

cards.def:
**Scout's older brother — four years ahead and starting to change.**
• Takes the Radley-house dare in chapter 1 — the summer's first trespass.
• By chapter 5 he is planning bigger risks with Dill, and Atticus is starting to notice.
cards.hint: Watch how much braver Jem gets once Dill is around for the summer.

cards.def:
**Their father, a lawyer — teaches by explanation, not punishment.**
• The empathy rule: you never really understand someone until you climb into his skin and walk around in it.
• Ends the fishing-pole plan with one line: stop tormenting that man.
cards.hint: Atticus never raises his voice in these chapters. Notice what he does instead.

cards.def:
**The summer friend from Meridian — small, dramatic, endlessly inventive.**
• The Boo Radley obsession is his idea first: the dares, the play-acting, the plans to make Boo come out.
• Talks big about a father he plainly doesn't really have around.
cards.hint: Dill supplies imagination; Maycomb supplies the legend.

cards.def:
**A man nobody has seen in years — the town filled the silence with a monster story.**
• The legend: six-and-a-half feet tall, eats raw squirrels, drools, stalks at night.
• One human-scale fact: as a teenager he got in trouble with the law, and his father chose to keep him home rather than send him away — he has been a near-total mystery to the town ever since.
cards.hint: Keep two columns: what is SAID about Boo, what anyone has actually SEEN him do.

cards.def:
**The Finches' cook — and the household's second parent.**
• Scolds Scout, not Walter, over the syrup: a guest is a guest, whatever he does to his dinner.
• Atticus treats her word as law, which tells you where she stands in the family.
cards.hint: Calpurnia's discipline is always about respect for someone else.

cards.def:
**The neighbor who talks to the children like people.**
• Azaleas, cake, and the sharpest tongue on the street.
• Knows more about the Radleys than anyone — and tells Scout it's the family's strict religion, not a curse, that shut the house up.
cards.hint: Miss Maudie answers Scout's Boo questions instead of shushing them.

cards.def:
**A tired old town where there is nowhere to go and nothing to buy — and no money to buy it with.**
• Scout nods at a president's line: nothing to fear but fear itself.
• Farm families like the Cunninghams live on trade, not cash.
cards.hint: The Depression isn't backdrop — it explains half the choices people make.

cards.def:
**A hole in the Radley oak that starts handing out small treasures.**
• Chapter 4: two sticks of gum, then two old Indian-head pennies.
• Nobody has explained it yet — Jem makes Scout rinse her mouth out with water, just in case.
cards.hint: 'So far' matters — the tree isn't finished giving yet.

cards.def:
**Climb into his skin and walk around in it — the book's engine, stated in chapter 3.**
• First test: Miss Caroline, the new teacher Scout wants to hate.
• Running test: Boo, whom everyone judges and no one knows.
cards.hint: Every chapter quietly asks: whose skin has Scout not tried on yet?

cards.def:
**The town tells one Boo story; the events tell another.**
• Legend: monster, prowler, phantom, a man with a knife.
• Evidence so far: two sticks of gum, two old pennies — quiet, small, unasked-for.
cards.hint: This gap is the novel in miniature. Keep score as it grows.

cards.def:
**Wishing harm; showing ill will.**
• Chapter 1 calls Boo a “malevolent phantom” — the town's word, not the evidence's.

**A legal knot that ties up land so the family can't freely sell or borrow against it.**
• Why Mr. Cunningham is land-rich, cash-poor — and pays Atticus in stovewood and hickory nuts.
cards.hint: Entailed land = frozen wealth. You can farm it, not spend it.

cards.def:
**An agreement where each side gives something up.**
• Atticus's deal in chapter 3: keep going to school, and we keep reading together every night — school's rules and Scout's reading both survive.
cards.hint: Atticus's compromises always cost him something too — that is why they work.

cards.def:
**A preference; a habitual liking for something.**
• Chapter 1 uses it wryly about the Radleys' unusual predilection: keeping to themselves.
cards.hint: Pre- = before: a leaning you bring to things in advance.

cards.def:
**A strict local sect Miss Maudie describes to Scout — they believe almost anything enjoyable is sinful.**
• They think Miss Maudie's flower garden is going straight to the devil, right along with her.
• Miss Maudie uses them to explain WHY the Radleys shut their doors, not just that they do.
cards.hint: A joke to Miss Maudie, a real clue to the reader: strict religion, not a monster, built that house's silence.

cards.def:
**Jem and Dill's plan to finally make contact with Boo — at night, through a shutter.**
• A note on the end of a fishing pole, meant to invite him out.
• Atticus catches them mid-attempt and ends it on the spot.
cards.hint: It is the boldest thing anyone has tried on the Radley house yet — bolder than a dare.

cards.def:
**List everything Boo has actually DONE, on the page, through chapter 5.**
• It should be a short list — that is the point.
• Now put it next to the six-and-a-half-foot, squirrel-eating legend. Worth saying out loud at dinner: why does a whole town prefer the scary version?
cards.hint: There is no wrong answer here. That is the point.

cards.def:
**Atticus told Jem and Dill, in plain words, to stop tormenting that man.**
• Prediction, before you read on: do they stop, or find a quieter way to keep going?
• Check back once you've read further. Being wrong about people is half of what this book is about.
cards.hint: Write your guess down somewhere. Future-you will want to compare.

questions.passage: “You never really understand a person until you consider things from his point of view … until you climb into his skin and walk around in it.”
questions.q: Atticus says this after Scout's disastrous first day of school. What is he actually asking her to do about Miss Caroline?
opts: Report her to the school board for banning reading
Prove her wrong by reading even more at school
Imagine the day from Miss Caroline's own side
Ignore her and keep reading at home in secret
questions.hint: Whose day was ALSO terrible in that classroom?
steps: Recall Miss Caroline's day: new in town, humiliated over the Cunningham quarter, alarmed by a cootie, corrected by a six-year-old who reads.
Atticus's advice is a method, not a verdict: stand where she stood before judging her.
From her side, the class's unwritten Maycomb rules were invisible — her mistakes were ignorance, not malice.
So the ask is empathy: hold your grudge until you have walked her day in her shoes.

ex.main: **Imagine the day from her side.** Atticus never says Miss Caroline was right — he says understanding comes before judgment. It is the novel's thesis, handed over in chapter 3.
ex.tip: When a quoted passage is a famous line, the question is almost never 'what does it say' — it is 'what does it ask someone to DO'.

questions.passage: “Boo was about six-and-a-half feet tall, judging from his tracks; he dined on raw squirrels and any cats he could catch …”
questions.q: Who gives this description, and what does the novel want you to notice about it?
opts: Jem — and every detail is invented; legend has completely replaced fact
Atticus — warning the children away from a dangerous man
Miss Maudie — teasing the children with a tall tale she made up
The adult narrator — reporting confirmed facts about Arthur Radley
questions.hint: 'Judging from his tracks' — has the speaker ever actually seen him?
steps: Place the line: chapter 1, the children trading Radley lore at the start of summer.
Check the evidence inside it: height guessed from tracks, diet from rumor — nobody has seen any of this.
That is Jem performing the legend for Dill, each retelling taller than the last.
The novel is showing you how a myth grows: confident details, zero witnesses.

ex.main: **Jem — and it is pure legend.** The tell is 'judging from his tracks': it admits, mid-sentence, that no one has ever seen the man being described.
ex.tip: When a description is vivid but sourceless, ask who benefits from telling it. Here: a boy impressing his audience.

questions.q: Put these chapter 1–5 events in the order they happen.
opts: Dill arrives for the summer and the Radley games begin
Scout's first day of school goes wrong for everyone
The first small gifts appear in the knothole
Atticus catches Jem and Dill with a note on a fishing pole
questions.hint: Summer, then school, then the tree starts giving — then the boldest try yet.
steps: Chapter 1 is summer: Dill arrives, the dares and Boo games start.
Chapter 2 is the calendar's next beat: school starts, and Scout's first day goes sideways.
Chapter 4: walking home from school, Scout finds gum, then pennies — the knothole starts giving.
Chapter 5: Jem and Dill's biggest move yet — a note on a fishing pole — and Atticus catches them in the act. Games, school, gifts, caught — that is the arc so far.

ex.main: **Dill and the games → first day of school → knothole gifts → the fishing-pole note.** Each step is a little bolder than the last, which is exactly the shape the summer is building.
ex.tip: Anchor order questions to the calendar the book gives you: summer first, school after.

questions.q: These four moments also happen in order across chapters 1–5. Put them in sequence.
opts: Jem takes the dare and touches the side of the Radley house
Scout finds two sticks of gum inside the oak tree's knothole
Miss Maudie tells Scout that a strict religion, not a monster, shut the Radleys' door
Atticus catches Jem and Dill trying to reach Boo with a note on a fishing pole
questions.hint: A dare, then a discovery, then an explanation, then getting caught.
steps: The dare is chapter 1 — the very first, smallest trespass against the house.
The gum in the knothole is chapter 4 — the first sign that something inside the Radley lot notices the children back.
Miss Maudie's explanation comes that same summer, earlier in chapter 5 than the fishing-pole plan — she reframes the legend before the boldest attempt happens.
The fishing-pole note is chapter 5's climax — the last and boldest try of the summer, the one that finally gets an adult's full attention.

ex.main: **Dare → gum in the knothole → Miss Maudie's explanation → the fishing-pole note.** Each event either escalates the children's boldness or reframes what they think they know, and the book alternates the two.
ex.tip: When two kinds of scenes repeat — action, then explanation — track them as one alternating sequence, not two separate ones.

questions.q: Three of these really happen in chapters 1–5. Which one is the lie?
opts: Two sticks of gum turn up inside the oak tree's knothole
Jem and Dill try to send Boo a note on the end of a fishing pole
Scout tumbles out of a rolling tire and lands against the Radley steps
Boo Radley chases the children off his porch with a kitchen knife
questions.hint: Check each against a scene you can point to on the page, not what Maycomb says.
steps: Test each statement against a scene you can name: the gum in the knothole is chapter 4 — true.
The fishing-pole note is chapter 5 — true, and it's what gets them caught.
The tire crashing onto the Radley steps is chapter 4 — true, and the closest anyone has been to the house all book.

A knife-chase? That's the LEGEND — scissors-in-the-leg lore about Boo's past, retold secondhand and years old. On the page, in chapters 1–5, Boo never actually appears. The lie is the one Maycomb would believe fastest.

ex.main: **The knife chase never happens.** Nobody has even seen Boo yet in these chapters — every 'fact' about him so far is legend, secondhand, or a small unexplained gift. That gap is the whole setup.
ex.tip: Spot-the-lie questions reward receipts: if you can't name the scene where it happened, suspect it.

questions.q: Walter Cunningham won't take Miss Caroline's quarter for lunch. Why?
opts: He already ate his lunch before school
He is afraid of the other children laughing at him
Cunninghams never take what they can't repay
He is planning to walk home for lunch
questions.hint: Scout tries to explain it: 'He's a Cunningham.'
steps: Scout tells Miss Caroline 'he's a Cunningham' as if that explains everything — in Maycomb, it does.
The Cunninghams are poor but square: they take nothing they can't repay, and a quarter is a debt.
So the refusal is dignity, not rudeness — which the newcomer teacher has no way to read.

ex.main: **Cunninghams never take what they can't pay back.** The quarter is charity, charity is debt, and debt is the one thing the family refuses to carry.
ex.tip: Poverty in this book comes in kinds — the Cunninghams' code is the measuring stick the novel will use later.

questions.q: Mr. Cunningham pays Atticus for legal work with stovewood, hickory nuts and turnip greens. What does this arrangement show?
opts: Atticus undercharges because the work was simple and quick
The Cunninghams are avoiding paying the full price
Entailment leaves them cash-poor, so they pay in goods
Atticus would rather be paid in goods than money
steps: The Cunningham problem is entailment: their land is legally tied up, so it can't be sold or borrowed against.
Farm goods are the only currency they actually have.
Atticus accepts the goods without comment and tells the children why — payment is payment when it is all a man has.
The arrangement shows both codes at once: Cunningham dignity and Atticus's respect for it.

ex.main: **Entailment leaves them land-rich and cash-poor, so they pay in goods.** Atticus treating stovewood as full payment is the same lesson as the refused quarter, seen from the other side.
ex.tip: When a book invents a payment scene, it is telling you about both parties — watch what the receiver does.

questions.q: Walter pours syrup all over his lunch, Scout objects loudly — and Calpurnia scolds SCOUT, not Walter. What is Calpurnia's rule?
opts: Never waste syrup during a Depression
A guest is treated with respect, whatever he does
Children should stay silent at the dinner table
Company manners only apply to grown-up visitors
steps: Walter's syrup is odd but harmless; Scout's mockery is what actually wounds someone at the table.
Calpurnia pulls Scout to the kitchen: he is 'yo' comp'ny' — your guest — and a guest is not to be shamed.
The rule is not about food. It is that hospitality outranks Scout's opinion of anyone's manners.

ex.main: **Guests get respect, whatever they do to their dinner.** Calpurnia's fury is aimed at the humiliation, not the syrup — the same dignity rule the Cunninghams live by, enforced at the Finch table.
ex.tip: In scenes with a 'wrong' character, check who the adult corrects. That points at the real offense.

questions.q: Atticus catches Jem and Dill trying to poke a note to Boo Radley through a shutter, on the end of a fishing pole. What is the real conflict in that scene?
opts: Whether fishing poles are allowed near the Radley fence
Their curiosity versus a living man's privacy and dignity
Whether the note was spelled correctly
Whether Dill is a bad influence on Jem and Scout
questions.hint: 'That man' — Atticus uses three words the children never use about Boo.
steps: To the children, Boo is a character to finally provoke into view — the summer's whole point.
Atticus's phrase 'that man' reclassifies him: not a legend, a neighbor who can likely hear every word.
The conflict is the book's empathy rule applied at home: their curiosity isn't harmless if it costs someone else his privacy.
Notice Atticus doesn't even ask what the note said — he doesn't need to. The method matters more than the message.

ex.main: **Curiosity versus a man's privacy and dignity.** The plan only works if Boo isn't real to them; Atticus's warning insists that he is — the skin-walking lesson, applied to their own front yard.
ex.tip: When an adult renames something in a scene — game to torment, phantom to man — the renaming IS the point.

questions.q: Miss Maudie tells Scout that Mr. Radley belongs to a group who believe almost any pleasure — even her flower garden — is sinful. What does this help explain?
opts: Why Miss Maudie has stopped gardening out of respect
Why the Radley house has stayed so shut off from the rest of Maycomb
Why Boo Radley is legally forbidden from leaving the house
Why the children are no longer allowed near the Radley yard
questions.hint: Miss Maudie is handing Scout an explanation that has nothing to do with monsters.
steps: Miss Maudie's line about the 'foot-washing Baptists' sounds like a joke about her garden — but she means more by it.
She is describing Mr. Radley's own strictness: a household that treats most of the outside world as something to keep out.
That strictness — not a curse, not a monster — is the actual, human reason the house stays closed.
It's the same move the whole novel keeps making: swap the scary explanation for the ordinary one, and the mystery gets smaller, not bigger.

ex.main: **It explains why the family shut its doors.** A rigid, joyless kind of religion is a plain, human reason — a much smaller story than the monster Maycomb prefers.
ex.tip: When a neighbor offers a boring explanation for a scary rumor, the book usually wants you to believe the boring one.

questions.q: After Atticus catches Jem and Dill with the fishing pole, what does he ask them to imagine, to make his point land?
opts: Imagine being sent to the principal's office for it
Imagine how they would feel if someone did the same to them
Imagine explaining the plan to Miss Maudie
Imagine what Boo Radley looks like up close
questions.hint: Atticus's go-to move all book is putting a person in someone else's spot — including his own sons.
steps: Atticus doesn't lecture about rules first — he asks Jem and Dill to switch places with the person they're bothering.
It's the exact method from chapter 3's advice about Miss Caroline, aimed at his own children this time.
The ask isn't 'would you get in trouble' — it's 'how would this feel done to you'.
That distinction is the whole empathy lesson, shrunk down to one small parenting moment.

ex.main: **How they'd feel if it happened to them.** Atticus never punishes first — he asks them to feel it from the other side, the same climb-into-his-skin move from chapter 3.
ex.tip: When a question asks how a character makes a point land, look for the METHOD, not just the words.

questions.q: Compared to most Maycomb adults in these chapters, how does Miss Maudie treat Scout and Jem?
opts: She mostly ignores them and keeps to her garden
She talks to them as equals and answers their real questions
She is stricter with them than their own father
She discourages their interest in the Radleys entirely
questions.hint: Compare how she handles Scout's Boo questions to how a strict teacher might.
steps: Most Maycomb adults in these chapters either scold the children (Miss Caroline) or feed the Boo legend (the neighborhood rumor mill).
Miss Maudie does neither: she lets Scout ask real questions and gives real, thought-through answers.
That includes the religion explanation — she could have brushed Scout off, and instead she explains her actual reasoning.
It's why Scout trusts her enough to keep asking, chapter after chapter.

ex.main: **She talks to them like people and actually answers.** Miss Maudie is the rare adult in these chapters who treats a child's curiosity as worth a real answer, not a scolding or a scary story.
ex.tip: When a character is defined by contrast, ask what everyone else in the scene does differently.

questions.q: According to the story passed around about Boo Radley's past, what did he do as a teenager that led to him being shut away at home?
opts: He ran away from Maycomb and lived with relatives for years
He got in trouble with the law, and his father kept him home instead
He was caught stealing from the general store downtown
He accidentally started a fire in the Radley smokehouse
questions.hint: This is chapter 1 — before any of the knothole or fishing-pole events.
steps: Chapter 1 gives Boo's backstory secondhand, the way the whole neighborhood tells it: trouble with the law as a teenager, alongside some other boys.
The other boys were sent to a state institution; Boo's father refused to let that happen to his own son.
Instead, Mr. Radley chose to keep him at home — and Boo has been almost entirely out of sight ever since.
That single choice is the actual origin of fifteen-plus years of silence, long before any legend added the squirrels and the six-and-a-half feet.

ex.main: **Trouble with the law, and a father who chose to keep him home rather than send him away.** Everything scarier that Maycomb has added since is legend built on top of one ordinary, sad decision.
ex.tip: When a legend has a real origin story, that origin is almost always smaller and sadder than the legend it grew into.

questions.passage: “… the Radley Place was inhabited by an unknown entity the mere description of whom was enough to make us behave for days on end; a malevolent phantom …”
opts: Impossible to see
Very old indeed
Wishing harm
Completely silent
steps: Break the word: mal- (bad) + volent (wishing, as in benevolent's opposite).
So malevolent = wishing harm.
Then catch the irony the book is planting: the 'malevolent phantom' spends chapters 1–5 leaving gum and pennies in a tree. The word belongs to the town, not the man.

ex.main: **Wishing harm.** Benevolent's evil twin. The chapter applies it to Boo in the same book that will spend 300 pages proving it wrong.
ex.tip: Vocabulary in novels is rarely neutral — check whether the story agrees with the word it just used.
